Beállítom Teljesen felépülhet a sérüléséből az a pilóta, aki hétfőn katapultált a balesetet szenvedő Gripenjéből , tudta meg az RTL . Az 51 éves katonát gerincsérülés miatt kellett műteni, az eljárás sikeres volt. A repülőgépet egy rendkívül tapasztalt, rendkívül jó fizikai állapotban lévő pilóta vezette, amelyik balesetet szenvedett a szolnoki katonai repülőtéren hétfőn. Eddig több mint kétezer órát repült, nemzetközi műveletekben is részt vett. A Gripenben meghibásodás történt , miközben éppen nagy sebességű elfogást gyakorolt. A repülőgépek Kecskemétről szálltak fel, oda-vissza megcsinálták a gyakorlatot, majd a második elfogás végén jöttek folyamatosan a hibaüzenetek, és elsötétültek a műszerek. A katona ekkor döntött úgy, hogy katapultál. Végül mentőhelikopterrel közvetlenül a Honvédkórházba szállították. Székely György, az Észak-Pesti Centrumkórház – Honvédkórház idegsebésze korábban azt mondta: a legnagyobb valószínűséggel a teljes felépülést biztosítja a balesetet szenvedett Gripen pilótájának a kisebb gerincműtét. Orvosi szempontból a katapultálás azért veszélyes, mert a kilövés nagy gyorsulást jelent, ami rendkívül megterhelő a szervezetre, elsősorban a gerinc sérülhet ilyenkor. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Nepali soldiers search for survivors in a hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa district, Nepal. Photograph: Prime Minister Secretariat, Nepal/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Nepali soldiers search for survivors in a hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa district, Nepal. Photograph: Prime Minister Secretariat, Nepal/AFP/Getty Images Nepal-Tibet flood disaster Nepal rescuers race to reach hundreds feared trapped in hydropower tunnels Workers thought to be stuck in underground areas at 11 sites after last week’s devastating flash floods Cait Kelly in Kathmandu and William Christou Mon 31 Aug 2026 11.56 EDT First published on Mon 31 Aug 2026 02.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Rescue teams are working to reach more than 900 missing hydropower workers, hundreds of whom are feared trapped in the tunnels and underground areas of 12 hydropower projects in Nepal after the devastating flash floods , ​the ⁠country’s disaster ​management authority has said. The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud ​and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to 939 people, with 16 more dead reported in Tibet. More than 4,400 are missing on the two sides of the border. About 500 of the missing hydropower workers at projects damaged by the flooding in Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts are thought to be trapped in tunnels built to control the flow of water. As rescue efforts drag on, experts fear the chances of finding survivors in tunnels are diminishing as oxygen levels fall. Some workers called for help when flooding started on Wednesday and those who had managed to escape tunnels said many of their colleagues were still trapped, said Mohan Kumar Dangi, the president of the Nepal Independent Power Producers’ Association. Devastated by floods and overwhelmed by bodies, Nepalis weep for what remains of their homes Read more Rescue efforts have been complicated by difficult terrain, persistently high flood waters and difficult weather. With more than 40 bridges destroyed, rescuers are relying on helicopters, while India and China are sending prefabricated truss bridges to help restore access. View image in fullscreen A resident examines his damaged home in Devighat, Nuwakot district. Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP The swollen Trishuli River has also continued to change course unpredictably, making planning a challenge. Areas that were dry one day are flooded the next, and further floods are a constant concern. Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, that were swept down the mountains by the torrent, have been buried in shallow graves after DNA testing on the plains ⁠of the Himalayan region. Nepali officials said on Monday that the focus was on reaching the 933 people missing from ‌hydropower plants. “A large amount of debris has been deposited and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels,” the Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told Reuters. About 250 people were rescued from the Upper Trishuli hydroelectric project over the weekend, and army engineers began blasting operations at the site to rescue another 42 workers thought be missing. View image in fullscreen A flood victim being airlifted from Rasuwa district yesterday to a hospital in Kathmandu. More than 4,400 people are now listed as missing. Photograph: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP/Getty Images The damage to hydropower infrastructure is estimated to have taken 700 megawatts out of service, about 10% of the country’s power capacity. Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams ⁠showed earth-moving equipment shovelling mud to try to reach the tunnels. Ashish Gurung, who normally works as a guide, was among the rescuers. “There is just mud everywhere,” he said. “Inside the tunnel it was worse. It’s so difficult to move, the mud is so deep.” His team was trying to access the Chilime hydropower plant in Rasuwa, one of the worst-hit areas. At least eight people are believed missing there, and an Indian team is working alongside the Nepali army using pumps and excavators to locate them. View image in fullscreen Ashish Gurung, left, with fellow rescue mountaineer Jenjen Lama at the Chilime hydropower plant in Rasuwa. Photograph: Supplied The Nepali prime minister, Balendra Shah, said rescue efforts were “challenging due to adverse weather, difficult terrain and ongoing risks.” Gurung said mountaineers were improvising by using planks of wood to check the depth of the mud, before using them as makeshift bridges along with a system of ropes to keep themselves safe. “Walking in it is very difficult, at one point it was up to our chests,” he said. “We got close to the first station, about 130 metres in. Inside that far … it looked like it was just bodies.” The hydropower company had given his team a map and it looked as if there was a chance people in the tunnels could have survived. “They have a safe area inside,” he said. “Some of them could potentially be alive. I am hoping they are alive.” Young girl rescued from rubble three days after Nepal flash flood – video The Red Cross estimates that more than 93,000 people have been affected by the disaster, heightening fears that the climate crisis is destabilising the geology of mountain and polar regions . Shah said the flood was an “unprecedented and devastating natural disaster” and that it was difficult to compile a complete assessment of the damage. “Despite the adverse weather, difficult terrain and continuing risks, we are moving forward with determination to save the lives of our citizens,” he said in a Facebook post late on Sunday. Almost 21,000 security personnel were involved in the rescue operations alongside civilian workers and volunteers, he said. Whole communities had been destroyed by the flooding, leaving families homeless in heavy rain. View image in fullscreen Rescuers work to access a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower plant in Nuwakot district, Nepal. Photograph: Nepal Army/Reuters “There are no roads, they have all been washed away, and many areas are just not accessible,” said a police officer coordinating rescue efforts in Nuwakot district. “It is very difficult for my men. The area is still flooded, and elsewhere it is all marshland.” Nepal’s disaster agency said on Monday it had counted 903 deaths, with 4,793 people, including 592 foreigners, missing. Chinese authorities had reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing as of Sunday. State media said 261 of the missing were foreigners, including more than 100 Nepalis. Among those missing are more than 30 British nationals. On Saturday, a rapid deployment team from the UK arrived in Nepal to support Britons and their families. The UK government has given a £5m support package to assist Nepal in its disaster response. Amid the soaring toll of death and missing was some hope. On Monday, rescuers pulled a six-year-old girl out of mud after hearing crying. “Her body was trapped in mud, but her head was outside,” the Nepali armed police spokesperson Netra Bahadur Karki told Agence France-Presse. China’s state-run CCTV said Beijing had mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated at least ​220m yuan (£24m) to support relief efforts and had been airdropping equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers, while its soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing. locator Nepal has said it does not need foreign help in general search and rescue operations, but it has leaned on its neighbours, India and China, for their expertise in tunnel rescues. Rescue operations have been suspended several times since Friday because of bad weather and concerns that a lake formed across the Nepal-China border by the disaster could trigger fresh flooding after it began overflowing into Nepal’s rivers. The weather was good on Monday, however, and rescue ⁠work picked up pace, said Narendra Pariyar, the district administrator of Rasuwa, one of the two hardest-hit districts. In the holy ​town of Devighat on the banks of the Trishuli, residents walked around the shells of what had once been ​homes , trying to salvage their belongings from the debris. View image in fullscreen People try to salvage belongings from their devastated homes in Devighat. Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, CCTV reported, saying ​it was a “new and prominent feature of cryosphere ‌disasters” on the Tibetan plateau. Two ​Nepali officials said China had ​not shared much information on glacier risks and water levels after a meeting to strengthen cooperation earlier this year, and they feared that could hamper future disaster preparedness. China’s foreign ministry said Beijing had continuously provided Nepal with meteorological and hydrological data and will continue to “strongly support” Nepal’s disaster relief efforts and safeguard the two countries’ common interests. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A British citizen who has been wanted by the FBI for more than 20 years has been arrested in Hungary . A 60-year-old man fled the United States in September 2004 while under investigation for child abuse, coercion and coercion for illegal sexual activity. An arrest warrant was issued for him in November of that year, and an international arrest warrant followed in 2006. On August 25 the Nemzeti Nyomozó Iroda (National Investigations Bureau) police received a tip from the FBI that the man might be travelling through Hungary. It was stopped close to Polgár while travelling on the M3 motorway, with police confirming the identity of the man. A 60-year-old British man has been arrested in Hungary (Image: Készenléti Rendőrség Nemzeti Nyomozó Iroda) He was arrested and taken to Hajdúnánás Police Station, where he was taken into custody. An extradition request was initiated but he was not remanded in custody, with the court releasing him. Hungarian police did not release the name of the man, and his image was not shown.
